subject: psychology
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Explanations of criminal behaviour (social learning and biological)
Making a criminal and reducing criminal behaviour
Core study: Bandura, Ross and Ross (1961)

questions.q: Which psychologists carried out the 1961 'Bobo doll' study of imitative aggression?
options: Bandura, Ross and Ross
Milgram, Ross and Zimbardo
Loftus, Palmer and Bandura
Raine, Ross and Bandura
questions.explain: The core study was conducted by Albert Bandura together with Dorothea Ross and Sheila Ross.

questions.q: In which year was the Bandura, Ross and Ross Bobo doll core study published?
questions.explain: The study was published in 1961.

questions.q: How many children took part in Bandura, Ross and Ross (1961)?
questions.explain: The sample was 72 children, made up of 36 boys and 36 girls.

questions.q: From where were the children in the Bobo doll study recruited?
options: Stanford University Nursery School
A prison in California
Yale University laboratory
Schools across the whole of the USA
questions.explain: The children were drawn from the Stanford University Nursery School.

questions.q: The children in the study were divided into three groups. Which set of conditions is correct?
options: Aggressive model, non-aggressive model, and a control group with no model
Reward, punishment, and no-consequence groups
Boys only, girls only, and mixed groups
Live model, filmed model, and cartoon model groups
questions.explain: Children saw either an aggressive adult model, a non-aggressive model, or no model at all (control).

questions.q: What did the study find about the influence of the model's sex on the children?
options: Children were more likely to imitate a same-sex model
Children only imitated female models
The sex of the model made no difference at all
Children imitated opposite-sex models more strongly
questions.explain: Imitation was stronger when the model was the same sex as the child, especially for boys with a male model.

questions.q: Which statement best summarises a key sex difference found in the results?
options: Boys showed more imitative physical aggression than girls
Girls were far more physically aggressive than boys
Boys and girls showed identical levels of physical aggression
Only girls imitated the aggressive model
questions.explain: Boys reproduced more physical aggression than girls, particularly after watching a male model.

questions.q: What did the results of the study most strongly support?
options: That aggression can be learned through observation and imitation
That aggression is entirely inherited through genes
That punishment always reduces aggression
That children cannot learn from adults
questions.explain: The findings supported social learning theory, showing aggressive behaviour can be learned by observing a model.

questions.q: According to social learning theory, criminal behaviour is mainly learned by which process?
options: Observing and imitating role models
Inheriting a criminal gene
Damage to the amygdala
Random chance
questions.explain: Social learning theory argues behaviour is learned by observing and imitating others, especially role models.

questions.q: What is meant by 'vicarious reinforcement' in social learning theory?
options: Learning by seeing another person rewarded for a behaviour
Being directly punished for your own actions
Inheriting behaviour from your parents
Learning through trial and error alone
questions.explain: Vicarious reinforcement is when we are more likely to copy a behaviour after seeing a model rewarded for it.

questions.q: Why might a young person be especially likely to imitate a particular role model?
options: Because they identify with the model and see them as similar or admirable
Because the model is always a stranger
Because they have never seen the behaviour before
Because imitation only happens with punishment
questions.explain: Identification with a model who seems similar, high-status or admired increases the likelihood of imitation.

questions.q: Which brain structure is linked in biological explanations to emotion and aggression?
options: The amygdala
The cerebellum
The retina
The cochlea
questions.explain: The amygdala is associated with processing emotion and is linked to aggressive behaviour.

questions.q: How does the biological explanation account for some criminal behaviour differing from the social learning explanation?
options: It focuses on brain structure, brain function and inherited genes rather than learning from others
It says all behaviour is copied from role models
It claims behaviour is only shaped by rewards and punishments
It argues the environment is the only cause
questions.explain: The biological approach explains crime through inherited genes and brain structure/function, not observation and imitation.

questions.q: A boy grows up in a household where older family members are praised by their friends for shoplifting, and he later shoplifts too. Which explanation best fits this?
options: Social learning theory through imitation and vicarious reinforcement
A biological explanation based on brain damage
An inherited genetic explanation
Pure random behaviour
questions.explain: Seeing admired models rewarded for crime and then copying them is imitation supported by vicarious reinforcement.

questions.q: A researcher finds that offenders in a sample show unusually low activity in the brain areas that control impulses. Which explanation does this best support?
options: The biological explanation of criminal behaviour
The social learning explanation
Vicarious reinforcement
Identification with a role model
questions.explain: Linking offending to brain function is a biological explanation of criminal behaviour.

questions.q: A token economy programme used to reduce offending is based on which principle?
options: Rewarding desirable behaviour with tokens that can be exchanged for privileges
Observing and imitating role models
Damage to the amygdala
Inherited criminal genes
questions.explain: Token economies use operant conditioning: desirable behaviour earns tokens that are later swapped for rewards.

questions.q: What is the main aim of an anger management programme for offenders?
options: To help offenders recognise and control the thoughts and feelings that trigger aggression
To reward offenders with tokens for good behaviour
To alter the offender's genes
To increase the offender's exposure to aggressive models
questions.explain: Anger management teaches offenders to identify triggers and use techniques to control their anger and aggression.

questions.q: Why can a token economy be described as using operant conditioning to change behaviour?
options: Because desirable behaviour is reinforced with rewards, making it more likely to be repeated
Because offenders observe and copy staff behaviour
Because it changes the structure of the brain
Because it relies on inherited genes
questions.explain: Reinforcing a behaviour with a reward to increase its frequency is the basis of operant conditioning.

questions.q: In a young offenders' unit, inmates earn tokens for tidying their rooms and attending classes, later exchanging them for extra recreation time. Which method is being used?
options: A token economy programme
An anger management programme
Social learning through role models
A biological treatment
questions.explain: Earning tokens for target behaviours and exchanging them for privileges is a token economy programme.

questions.q: A prison psychologist notices an offender's aggression is usually set off by feeling disrespected, and teaches him to spot this trigger and use calming techniques. Which approach is this?
options: Anger management
A token economy
Vicarious reinforcement
A genetic explanation
questions.explain: Identifying triggers for aggression and learning techniques to control the response is anger management.
